articles.title: Scientists find water was fueling volcanoes 3 billion years ago
articles.summary: Ancient rocks from Western Australia suggest water was reaching deep inside Earth more than three billion years ago, long before modern plate tectonics may have fully developed. Researchers propose that water-rich pieces of crust periodically sank into the mantle through a process they call “dripduction.” The buried water then helped produce magma and volcanic eruptions.
articles.content:
Geologists studying some of Earth's oldest volcanic rocks have found evidence that water was already influencing the planet's interior and helping drive volcanic activity more than three billion years ago.

The international team, led by Adelaide University geochemist Dr. Eric Vandenburg, examined ancient rocks from Western Australia's Pilbara Craton. Their analysis suggests that water had traveled far beneath the surface before contributing to the formation of magma that fed volcanoes resembling those found around the Pacific "Ring of Fire" today.

Published in Nature Communications, the findings indicate that Earth may have been recycling water between its surface and interior much earlier than scientists had realized, even though the young planet operated very differently from the world we know now.

A Rare Look at the Young Earth

Dr. Vandenburg, from the School of Physics, Chemistry and Earth Sciences, said the ancient rocks offer an unusual opportunity to investigate conditions on Earth billions of years ago.

"These rocks formed more than three billion years ago, when Earth was a very different place," he said.

Today, plate tectonics plays a central role in moving water through the planet. At subduction zones, one tectonic plate sinks beneath another, carrying water from the oceans down toward the mantle. That water can help generate magma, which rises toward the surface and contributes to the volcanoes that help build continents.

"The early Earth was too hot for plates to behave that way, so until now it has been unclear whether surface water could have made that journey more than three billion years ago, and if so, how.

"What surprised us was finding evidence that large amounts of water had already made their way deep into the Earth's interior and influenced the formation of volcanic rocks."

A Process Called "Dripduction"

The researchers suggest that another geological mechanism may have moved water into the mantle before modern plate tectonics became established.

They call the process "dripduction." In this scenario, dense, water-rich portions of Earth's cooler outer crust periodically sagged downward and collapsed into the hotter mantle, transporting water with them.

As those sections of crust descended, they released their water into the mantle. That water then helped generate magma, which eventually rose, erupted through volcanoes, and cooled into rocks that have survived for billions of years.

"The Earth wasn't operating exactly as it does now, but it appears some of the key processes were already in place," Dr. Vandenburg said.

When Did Earth Begin Recycling Its Surface?

The discovery addresses a major question in geology: how early did materials begin moving between Earth's surface and its deep interior?

Pinpointing when water first started traveling deep underground matters because this recycling process affects volcanic activity, the growth of continents, and the movement of ingredients that are important for life.

The findings may also help scientists better understand how Earth's continents developed and how the planet gradually evolved into its modern form.

Chemical Clues From 3.1 Billion Years Ago

Rocks from this period are extremely rare, which makes the Pilbara especially valuable. The region contains some of the best-preserved rocks from the early Earth, giving researchers a rare record of processes that occurred billions of years ago.

By studying chemical signatures locked inside the rocks, the team was able to reconstruct geological events dating back roughly 3.1 billion years.

The results suggest that Earth's surface and deep interior were interacting much earlier than previously recognized. Rather than being relatively static, the young planet appears to have been surprisingly dynamic and was already recycling one of its most essential substances: water.

The study involved researchers from Adelaide University, Monash University, the Geological Survey of Western Australia, Curtin University, the Australian National University, Cardiff University and the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research in Germany.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about Earth's early water cycle and volcanic activity, revealing that water was recycled deep inside Earth over 3 billion years ago through a newly proposed geological process called 'dripduction.' This finding advances understanding of Earth's geological and environmental evolution, with broad implications for planetary science and the origins of life, representing a meaningful breakthrough in Earth sciences.

articles.title: Battle to save the tiny, gooey snail only found in one lake in the UK
articles.summary: Once prevalent across the UK, this mollusc is now only found in one lake in Wales.
articles.content:
A tiny snail found in only one lake in the UK has been dubbed as precious as an Egyptian artefact as conservationists bid to save it.

Several British zoos are setting up so-called ark populations of the glutinous snail, one of Europe's rarest species, using creatures bred in a back garden in Ceredigion.

"Beguiled by their cuteness," conservationist Ian Hughes has made it his "life-defining" mission to protect the threatened mollusc, which was once widespread in UK waters.

"There was a point where we'd got more snails in our garden than have ever been seen in the wild," he said.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful conservation effort to save one of Europe's rarest snail species, which has a positive environmental impact and broad significance for biodiversity preservation. The story is focused on a single topic with clear context about the species' rarity and the conservation actions being taken.
articles.personality_title: Conservationists race to save rare snail found only in one Welsh lake
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – A tiny snail species, once common across the UK, now lives only in a single lake in Wales. This snail is very rare and is considered one of the rarest in Europe.

**What happened** – Conservationists, including British zoos, are working to protect this tiny snail called the glutinous snail. They have started breeding the snails in a garden in Ceredigion, Wales, and are creating special groups called ark populations to keep the species safe.

**Impact** – This effort is important because the snail is now almost extinct in the wild. Saving it helps protect biodiversity, which means keeping many different kinds of animals and plants alive. The work shows how people can help even the smallest creatures survive.

**What's next step** – The conservation teams will continue breeding the snails and plan to release them carefully back into their natural lake when it is safe. They also hope other zoos will join to help increase the snail’s numbers.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A rare snail found only in one Welsh lake is being saved through careful breeding and teamwork by conservationists and zoos.

articles.title: El Niño goes viral — and scientists learn what makes people care about the climate
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02763-3Evoking emotions is more likely to prompt people to engage with climate efforts than are data alone.
articles.content:
Glaciers shape the landscapes of Spitsbergen, an island of Norway’s Svalbard archipelago in the Arctic Ocean.Credit: Arterra/Sven-Erik Arndt/UIG/Getty

As warnings about a potential ‘mega’ El Niño grab headlines and spread through social media, communicators face a familiar challenge: how to persuade people to pay attention to climate risks — and act.

Fighting climate change takes more than data — it needs wonder, love and hope

A study, now published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology, suggests that emotionally engaging forms of communication are more effective than scientific facts alone in motivating climate action1. But messages focused on individual responsibility had little impact — and sometimes backfired.

“Our findings show that merely providing scientific facts is not the best way to communicate on climate-related issues — you need to connect with people,” says co-author Tobias Brosch, a psychologist at the University of Geneva, Switzerland.

“The emotions you feel when you watch a nature documentary, see the Northern Lights or witness the birth of a new animal imbue these events with meaning,” he adds. “They may also drive you to look better after our environment — by volunteering your time, donating or voting for climate-friendly parties.”

Inspiring awe

The study combined and analysed 71 publications, and included at least 216,000 participants who had been involved in experimental tests of the effect of different public communication methods on climate-related behaviours, such as making charity donations or stating intentions to reduce their carbon footprint in later interviews.

“We wanted to integrate all the scientific literature that has evaluated climate-change communication formats, and then look at impacts that interested us, which is climate action, climate-policy support or climate intentions,” says Brosch.

Most of the communication strategies went some way towards prompting climate action. Fact-based messaging — such as explaining the greenhouse-gas effect — increased the likelihood of people engaging with climate efforts. But communications designed to evoke emotions, such as awe at the beauty of nature and fear of the threats it is facing, were among the most successful.

The study shows the pivotal role of stories in communication, says Nicholas Epley, a behavioural scientist at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business in Illinois. “We reason in stories and concrete experiences: facts aren’t nearly as persuasive as individual stories, particularly when there’s distrust,” he says.

The analysis also showed what didn’t work: reminding individuals of their personal responsibility to act on climate change did little to convince people to mobilize, and even produced retaliation. This is consistent with what other initiatives have found. For example, during Earth Hour — a global event run by the WWF charity that recommends everyone turn their lights off for an hour — some organizations turn on all their lights in defiance.

“It possibly creates reactance, mistrust or this over-saturation of ‘oh, come on, now this is also my responsibility?’,” says Brosch. “Whereas the ones that worked went via an emotional pathway – ‘look, this is what’s worth fighting for’.”

Thijs Bouman, an environmental psychologist at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, says that although the study’s effect sizes are relatively small, they can still be meaningful, particularly for large-scale communication activities. “Sometimes governments and decision makers ask for an intervention that will immediately make a substantial change, but this study shows it is obviously very unrealistic,” he says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant scientific study that identifies effective communication strategies to inspire public engagement and action on climate change, a major global issue. It provides detailed insights into how emotional engagement rather than just facts can motivate climate action, which has broad societal impact and potential to improve environmental outcomes.
articles.personality_title: Study finds emotions motivate climate action more than facts alone
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Climate change is a big problem that needs people to care and take action. But it’s hard to get everyone to pay attention and do something about it. Scientists wanted to know the best way to communicate about climate risks, especially during events like the El Niño weather pattern.

**What happened** – Researchers looked at 71 studies involving over 216,000 people to see which ways of talking about climate change made people more likely to help or change their behavior. They found that messages that made people feel emotions like awe or worry about nature worked better than just sharing facts or telling people they were personally responsible.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows that simply giving scientific information isn’t enough. People connect more with stories and feelings, like seeing beautiful nature or hearing about threats to it. On the other hand, messages that blame individuals can make people push back and ignore the problem. This helps groups and governments understand how to inspire real action.

**What’s next step** – Scientists and communicators can now create campaigns that focus on emotional connection, using stories and images that inspire wonder and care for the environment. This approach can be used in schools, social media, and public events to encourage more people to support climate-friendly choices and policies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Connecting with people’s emotions, not just facts, is key to encouraging climate action and helping the planet.

articles.title: The slow, muddy work of saving ancient bogs
articles.summary: Sarah Hickey and her team help keep nearly 20,000 acres of upland in the Isle of Man healthy.
articles.content:
High up on a Manx hillside, Sarah Hickey effortlessly pushes a metre-long metal rod into the wet ground until it disappears almost to her hands.

"This is pretty deep here," she says, reading the markings on the probe. Beneath her boots is peat, built up over thousands of years and consisting of partially decayed plants and organic matter.

Hickey is the island's Peatland Officer and part of an Uplands team of just three, who, between them, manage about 8,000 hectares of the Island's hills.

Hickey's job is to find the parts of that landscape which have been damaged, and inject life into it.

Peat is partially decomposed vegetation that builds up in waterlogged ground over centuries, storing more carbon than any other soil on Earth.

"It's important to keep that carbon locked away and not released to the atmosphere," Hickey says.

Much of that carbon has stayed locked away, but not all of it. The island's uplands were largely stripped of trees by the 17th century, and with little timber left to burn, islanders turned to the hills for fuel instead.

Peat would be cut into blocks and left to dry; peat made a good, slow-burning fuel, and for generations it was what Manx households cooked on and heated their homes with.

The practice was banned in 2020, but the bare faces that cutting left behind are still collapsing and eroding today, washing sediment down into reservoirs.
articles.reasoning: The article describes active conservation efforts to restore and protect ancient peatlands on the Isle of Man, which store significant carbon and help mitigate climate change. This work has broad environmental significance and tangible positive impact on carbon storage and ecosystem health.
articles.personality_title: Saving ancient peatlands: Protecting the Isle of Man’s natural carbon stores
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – On the Isle of Man, a small island in the Irish Sea, the upland areas are covered with peat, a type of soil made of partly decayed plants that has built up over thousands of years. Peatlands store more carbon than any other soil type, helping to keep carbon locked away and out of the atmosphere.

**What happened** – Sarah Hickey, the island’s Peatland Officer, and her small team manage about 8,000 hectares (nearly 20,000 acres) of upland peatlands. They work to find damaged areas caused by past peat cutting and restore them. Peat was once widely cut for fuel until this was banned in 2020. The team uses tools like metal probes to measure peat depth and identify places that need repair.

**Impact** – Protecting and restoring peatlands is important because it stops stored carbon from being released into the air, which helps slow climate change. The work also reduces erosion that can harm water supplies. By fixing damaged peatlands, the team supports the health of the island’s natural environment and helps keep carbon safely stored.

**What’s next step** – The team will continue restoring damaged peatlands and preventing further erosion. Their work may inspire other places with peatlands to protect these important areas. Over time, the restored peatlands will grow thicker and healthier, keeping more carbon locked underground.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A small team on the Isle of Man is carefully restoring ancient peatlands to protect vital carbon stores and improve the island’s environment.
articles.personality_title_fr: Sauver les tourbières anciennes : protéger les réserves naturelles de carbone de l’île de Man
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Sur l’île de Man, une petite île en mer d’Irlande, les zones de haute altitude sont couvertes de tourbe, un type de sol formé de plantes partiellement décomposées sur des milliers d’années. Les tourbières stockent plus de carbone que tout autre sol, aidant à garder ce carbone enfermé et hors de l’atmosphère.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Sarah Hickey, responsable des tourbières de l’île, et son équipe gèrent environ 8 000 hectares (près de 20 000 acres) de tourbières en haute altitude. Ils cherchent les zones endommagées par la coupe de tourbe passée et les restaurent. La coupe de tourbe, autrefois utilisée comme combustible, a été interdite en 2020. L’équipe utilise des sondes métalliques pour mesurer la profondeur de la tourbe et repérer les endroits à réparer.

**Impact** – Protéger et restaurer les tourbières est important car cela empêche le carbone stocké d’être libéré dans l’air, ce qui aide à ralentir le changement climatique. Ce travail réduit aussi l’érosion qui peut abîmer les réserves d’eau. En réparant les tourbières, l’équipe soutient la santé de l’environnement naturel de l’île et garde le carbone en sécurité.

articles.personality_title_es: Salvar las turberas antiguas: proteger las reservas naturales de carbono en la Isla de Man
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En la Isla de Man, una pequeña isla en el Mar de Irlanda, las zonas altas están cubiertas de turba, un tipo de suelo formado por plantas parcialmente descompuestas durante miles de años. Las turberas almacenan más carbono que cualquier otro suelo, ayudando a mantener ese carbono guardado y fuera de la atmósfera.

**Qué pasó** – Sarah Hickey, la responsable de turberas de la isla, y su pequeño equipo gestionan alrededor de 8,000 hectáreas (casi 20,000 acres) de turberas en las tierras altas. Buscan áreas dañadas por la antigua extracción de turba y las restauran. La extracción de turba, que se usaba como combustible, se prohibió en 2020. El equipo usa sondas metálicas para medir la profundidad de la turba y encontrar lugares que necesitan reparación.

**Impacto** – Proteger y restaurar las turberas es importante porque evita que el carbono almacenado se libere al aire, lo que ayuda a frenar el cambio climático. También reduce la erosión que puede dañar las reservas de agua. Al reparar las turberas, el equipo apoya la salud del ambiente natural de la isla y mantiene el carbono seguro.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo seguirá restaurando turberas dañadas y previniendo la erosión. Su trabajo podría inspirar a otros lugares con turberas a proteger estas áreas importantes. Con el tiempo, las turberas restauradas crecerán más gruesas y saludables, almacenando más carbono.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un pequeño equipo en la Isla de Man está restaurando cuidadosamente turberas antiguas para proteger reservas vitales de carbono y mejorar el entorno de la isla.
